title: All beings in the self
hookLine: one who sees all beings in the self and the self in all beings hates no one (Isha Upanishad 6)
tomorrow: what's hiding the truth? the Isha says it's made of gold.

cards: There's often one: the coworker who chews loudly, the neighbor with the leaf blower, the person whose posts make your jaw tighten. Could you see yourself in them? The Isha Upanishad says that's exactly the point.

One who sees all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, hates no one. Hindu teachers read that verse in more than one way, and argue about it. To see why, start with a father, a son, and a cup of salt water.

teach.h: SALTY AT THE TOP, MIDDLE, BOTTOM.
teach.b: In the Chandogya Upanishad, Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu to drop salt in water overnight. Morning: bring me the salt. He can't find it.
Sip from the top. Salty. From the middle.
It's everywhere, unseen. That fine essence is the Self of all this, says the father. That you are, Shvetaketu: tat tvam asi.
Now two readings, both inside Hindu tradition. Let both speak. Shankara's Advaita: the Self in you and the Self of all beings are one and the same.
Hate needs a second person, and in the deepest truth there isn't one. That's why the verse says hates no one: there's no one else to hate.
Ramanuja's reading: the Lord dwells in every being as its inner Self, the way a soul dwells in a body. Beings are real, distinct and loved, and each one is the Lord's own body.
You don't hate them because you'd be hating where God lives.
One says no other; the other says every other is holy.

teach.h: RAMANUJA: EVERY BEING THE LORD'S BODY.
teach.b: Both land on the same three words.
Both schools take the verse seriously enough to disagree about it.

how: Hindus study the Isha and Chandogya Upanishads in the schools of Vedanta; Advaita, following Shankara, and Vishishtadvaita, following Ramanuja, read 'that you are' and 'the Self in all beings' differently.

games.q: what does “all beings in the self” mean?
o: keeping your own self at the center of every choice
loving only those who share your own beliefs
seeing every creature held in one Self, and that Self in each

games.q: salt, son and two readings: tap the pairs.
p: the father with the salt water
every being is the Lord's body

s: 'see the Self in all beings' means every Hindu school teaches you and God are identical
Advaita reads it that way; Ramanuja reads it as the Lord dwelling in every distinct being.
in the Chandogya, the salt is unseen but tastes the same from top to bottom
Uddalaka uses it to show the fine essence that pervades everything: that you are.
the Isha says hates no one is a feeling you force yourself to have
it says it follows from seeing: one who sees all beings in the Self hates no one.

games.q: you lean toward Shankara's reading. to argue fairly, state the best case for Ramanuja's side.
o: beings are real and loved, each the Lord's body; you honor them, not dissolve them.
people are basically illusions, so it doesn't matter how you treat them.
only holy people carry the Lord within; others can be ignored.
games.why: Ramanuja keeps every being real and distinct, and makes each one holy as the Lord's body. that's why it hates no one, too.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one stranger you saw today, or someone you find hard to stand. Notice they breathe as you breathe, in and out, right now somewhere.
Rest there, and let the one Self, or the Lord within, as you understand it, be in them too.

wordCard.voice: All beings in the self: the Isha's sixth verse, seeing every being in the Self and the Self in every being.

orig.say: SAR-vuh BHOO-tay-shoo CHAHT-mah-num TUH-toh nuh vi-joo-GOOP-suh-tay
orig.note: Sanskrit, Isha Upanishad 6: and the Self in all beings, then one shrinks from none.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: hates no one, whichever way you read it. Three verses into the Isha.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 6 (one who sees all beings in the Self and the Self in all beings shrinks from none)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.13 (Uddalaka, Shvetaketu and the salt in water; tat tvam asi)
Shankara, commentaries on Isha 6 and Chandogya 6.8–16; Ramanuja, Vedartha Sangraha and Sri Bhashya (the Lord as the inner Self of all beings, who are his body)
